items.narrative_markdown:
# Birthplace of Elizabeth Mariah (Turnbow) Barker (c. 1823)

**Conclusion (Probable):** Elizabeth, wife of the English-born blacksmith and farmer Jonathan Barker of Jasper and Smith counties, Mississippi, was born about 1823 in **Alabama**, not England. The FamilySearch tree records her as Elizabeth Mariah Turnbow (KWJ6-RPH). The "England" birthplace attached to her comes from an indexing error.

## The problem

The online index to the 1850 U.S. census for Jasper County, Mississippi, gives Elizabeth Barker's birthplace as England.[1] Later records give Alabama, and one daughter said Mississippi. Her birthplace decides where to look for her birth family.

## The evidence

**1850 — the original page.** On the handwritten 1850 schedule, the Barker household reads: Jonathan Barker, 30, blacksmith, born *England*; Elizabeth, 27, born *Alabama*; Sarah Martha, 4, born *Mississippi*; Amanda P., 2.[2] The informant is not named; in practice it was usually the wife or husband. This is an original record.

**Her own household, 1860-1880.** Every later census of the household gives Alabama for Elizabeth: 1860 Smith County (about age 36),[3] 1870 Smith County (about 47),[4] and 1880 Raleigh, Smith County (56, wife of "John" Barker, born England).[5] Each was taken by a different enumerator. All of these answers come from Elizabeth's own household, so they show one consistent family answer over thirty years.

**Her daughters.** In 1880, daughter Martha S. (Sarah Martha) Lovett lived next door to the Barkers. She gave her father's birthplace as England and her mother's as **Alabama**.[5] Daughter Amanda Ainsworth, in another part of Smith County, gave her mother's birthplace as **Mississippi** in 1880 and 1910.[6][8] In 1900 she gave Mississippi for both parents, although her father was English.[7]

**The Turnbow family (context).** The tree names her parents as Robert F. Turnbow and Sarah Canterberry, married in September 1816 in Madison County, Mississippi Territory, an area that became part of Alabama in 1817. No record found here states that they were Elizabeth's parents. This is context only and is not used to prove the birthplace.

## Resolving the conflict

*England* is not testimony at all. It exists only in the modern index, and on the original page it sits on Jonathan's line. The indexer moved the birthplace column down one row: Elizabeth received her husband's "England," Sarah Martha received Elizabeth's "Alabama," and Amanda received Sarah Martha's "Mississippi."[1][2]

*Mississippi* is a second-hand answer from one daughter, repeated across three censuses with the same informant. One of those entries is plainly wrong about her father. Amanda grew up in Mississippi among relatives settled there since about 1830, and the family's earlier home in Madison County had been part of the Mississippi Territory. A child reporting a parent's birthplace from family memory could easily give that answer.

*Alabama* comes from the original 1850 page and three later censuses of Elizabeth's own household. Her next-door daughter gave the same answer.

## Limits

The tier is **probable**, not proved. Only the 1850 entry has been examined in the original. The 1860-1880 Barker entries were read from indexes. No record names the informant, and no record gives a county of birth. A county could come from an obituary, a Bible record, the original LDS record-of-members register for the Mississippi Conference, or the original 1860-1880 census pages. This conclusion does not establish her parentage, which needs its own research question.

## Sources

1. "United States, Census, 1850," index, FamilySearch, Elizabeth Barker in household of Jonathan Barker, Jasper, Mississippi (ark:/61903/1:1:M4L8-3SY).
2. 1850 U.S. census, Jasper Co., Mississippi, population schedule, image 73 of 104, Jonathan Barker household; FamilySearch image ark:/61903/3:1:S3HY-DC1S-623.
3. "United States, Census, 1860," FamilySearch, Elizabeth Barker in household of Jonathan Barker, Smith, Mississippi (ark:/61903/1:1:M6GV-MGR).
4. "United States, Census, 1870," FamilySearch, Elizabeth Barker, Smith, Mississippi (ark:/61903/1:1:MFSR-DYF).
5. "United States, Census, 1880," FamilySearch, Raleigh, Smith, Mississippi, sheet 295C-D, John and Elisabeth Barker and Major W. and Martha S. Lovett households (ark:/61903/3:1:33S7-9YB8-HDX).
6. 1880 U.S. census, Smith Co., Mississippi, Beat 2, ED 104, sheet 310C, Asbery Ainsworth household; FamilySearch image ark:/61903/3:1:33SQ-GYB8-WKM.
7. "United States, Census, 1900," FamilySearch, Mandy P Ainsworth, Beat 2 Summerland, Smith, Mississippi (ark:/61903/1:1:M9FS-YK8).
8. "United States, Census, 1910," FamilySearch, Amanda P Ainsworth, Taylorsville, Smith, Mississippi (ark:/61903/1:1:MPDG-3ZJ).

items.narrative_markdown:
# Birthplace of Elizabeth Mariah (Turnbow) Barker (c. 1823)

**Conclusion (Probable):** Elizabeth, wife of the English-born blacksmith and farmer Jonathan Barker of Jasper and Smith counties, Mississippi, was born about 1823 in **Alabama**, not England. The FamilySearch tree records her as Elizabeth Mariah Turnbow (KWJ6-RPH). The "England" birthplace attached to her comes from an indexing error.

## The problem

The online index to the 1850 U.S. census for Jasper County, Mississippi, gives Elizabeth Barker's birthplace as England.[1] Later records give Alabama, and one daughter said Mississippi. Her birthplace decides where to look for her birth family.

## The evidence

**1850 — the original page.** On the handwritten 1850 schedule, the Barker household reads: Jonathan Barker, 30, blacksmith, born *England*; Elizabeth, 27, born *Alabama*; Sarah Martha, 4, born *Mississippi*; Amanda P., 2.[2] The informant is not named; in practice it was usually the wife or husband. This is an original record.

**Her own household, 1860-1880.** Every later census of the household gives Alabama for Elizabeth: 1860 Smith County (about age 36),[3] 1870 Smith County (about 47),[4] and 1880 Raleigh, Smith County (56, wife of "John" Barker, born England).[5] Each was taken by a different enumerator. All of these answers come from Elizabeth's own household, so they show one consistent family answer over thirty years.

**Her daughters.** In 1880, daughter Martha S. (Sarah Martha) Lovett lived next door to the Barkers. She gave her father's birthplace as England and her mother's as **Alabama**.[5] Daughter Amanda Ainsworth, in another part of Smith County, gave her mother's birthplace as **Mississippi** in 1880 and 1910.[6][8] In 1900 she gave Mississippi for both parents, although her father was English.[7]

**The Turnbow family (context).** The tree names her parents as Robert F. Turnbow and Sarah Canterberry, married in September 1816 in Madison County, Mississippi Territory, an area that became part of Alabama in 1817. No record found here states that they were Elizabeth's parents. This is context only and is not used to prove the birthplace.

## Resolving the conflict

*England* is not testimony at all. It exists only in the modern index, and on the original page it sits on Jonathan's line. The indexer moved the birthplace column down one row: Elizabeth received her husband's "England," Sarah Martha received Elizabeth's "Alabama," and Amanda received Sarah Martha's "Mississippi."[1][2]

*Mississippi* is a second-hand answer from one daughter, repeated across three censuses with the same informant. One of those entries is plainly wrong about her father. Amanda grew up in Mississippi among relatives settled there since about 1830, and the family's earlier home in Madison County had been part of the Mississippi Territory. A child reporting a parent's birthplace from family memory could easily give that answer.

*Alabama* comes from the original 1850 page and three later censuses of Elizabeth's own household. Her next-door daughter gave the same answer.

## Limits

The tier is **probable**, not proved. Only the 1850 entry has been examined in the original. The 1860-1880 Barker entries were read from indexes. No record names the informant, and no record gives a county of birth. A county could come from an obituary, a Bible record, the original LDS record-of-members register for the Mississippi Conference, or the original 1860-1880 census pages. This conclusion does not establish her parentage, which needs its own research question.

## Sources

1. "United States, Census, 1850," index, FamilySearch, Elizabeth Barker in household of Jonathan Barker, Jasper, Mississippi (ark:/61903/1:1:M4L8-3SY).
2. 1850 U.S. census, Jasper Co., Mississippi, population schedule, image 73 of 104, Jonathan Barker household; FamilySearch image ark:/61903/3:1:S3HY-DC1S-623.
3. "United States, Census, 1860," FamilySearch, Elizabeth Barker in household of Jonathan Barker, Smith, Mississippi (ark:/61903/1:1:M6GV-MGR).
4. "United States, Census, 1870," FamilySearch, Elizabeth Barker, Smith, Mississippi (ark:/61903/1:1:MFSR-DYF).
5. "United States, Census, 1880," FamilySearch, Raleigh, Smith, Mississippi, sheet 295C-D, John and Elisabeth Barker and Major W. and Martha S. Lovett households (ark:/61903/3:1:33S7-9YB8-HDX).
6. 1880 U.S. census, Smith Co., Mississippi, Beat 2, ED 104, sheet 310C, Asbery Ainsworth household; FamilySearch image ark:/61903/3:1:33SQ-GYB8-WKM.
7. "United States, Census, 1900," FamilySearch, Mandy P Ainsworth, Beat 2 Summerland, Smith, Mississippi (ark:/61903/1:1:M9FS-YK8).
8. "United States, Census, 1910," FamilySearch, Amanda P Ainsworth, Taylorsville, Smith, Mississippi (ark:/61903/1:1:MPDG-3ZJ).

Based on the project file, here's a clear picture of where the Flynn research stands and which unindexed image volumes should be prioritized next.

---

## Flynn Research — Unindexed Browse Strategy

### Current State at a Glance

| What's done | Gap |
|---|---|
| 1850 & 1860 censuses (Patrick in Thomas Flynn household) | 1860–1908 entirely undocumented |
| Patrick's 1908 death certificate (names Thomas as father) | Patrick's mother unknown |
| Thomas Flynn's 1881 will — rough citation found (src_006) | Full probate packet not yet browsed |
| Thomas → Patrick 1881 deed found (src_008) | Thomas Flynn's origins unknown |
| Patrick's 1845 baptism at St. Mary's, Pottsville (src_005) | Thomas Flynn's marriage record not found |
| Proof rated **Probable** — needs corroboration to reach **Proved** | Naturalization record for Thomas not searched |

---

### Recommended Browse Order

#### 🥇 Priority 1 — Schuylkill County Will Books (pli_006, already "in_progress")

**Why first:** The will of Thomas Flynn (1881) is already cited as src_006, but only the cover/index entry has been seen. The **full will text** is almost certainly an unindexed image volume. A will naming Patrick, siblings, and a wife would upgrade the proof from *Probable* to *Proved*.

**What to browse:** Schuylkill County Will Books on FamilySearch — navigate to the volume covering 1878–1885, find Thomas Flynn's entry, and read the full document including any attached inventory or accounts of administration (those are often in a separate Orphans' Court docket volume).

**What to look for:**
- Direct naming of Patrick Flynn as "son" — this single finding closes the question
- Names of Patrick's mother (Thomas's wife)
- Names of siblings → additional corroboration lines

---

#### 🥈 Priority 2 — St. Mary's Catholic Church Marriage Register, Pottsville (1830s–1845)

**Why:** Patrick's baptism at St. Mary's is already in the project (src_005, 1845). The **marriage register** for the same parish — likely 1838–1845 given Patrick's birth year — would document Thomas Flynn's marriage and name his wife, establishing Patrick's mother. Irish Catholic immigrant families in the Pennsylvania anthracite region almost universally married in a Catholic church.

**What to browse:** FamilySearch has digitized Catholic parish registers for several Pennsylvania dioceses. Search for St. Mary's, Pottsville (Schuylkill County) under Pennsylvania, Diocese of Philadelphia (pre-1868) or Diocese of Scranton records. Marriage registers are rarely indexed but are browsable image-by-image.

**What to look for:**
- Thomas Flynn marriage entry, ~1840–1845
- Bride's name → Patrick's mother
- Witnesses → may be relatives, neighbors, or persons who appear in other records

---

#### 🥉 Priority 3 — Schuylkill County Naturalization Records (Court of Common Pleas, 1840s–1860s)

**Why:** Thomas Flynn emigrated from Ireland before 1845 (Patrick was born ~1845 and enumerated in Schuylkill County in 1850). Thomas's **declaration of intent** and/or **petition for naturalization** would name his country of origin, and sometimes his county or townland in Ireland, his wife's name, and children. This is an often-overlooked source with high genealogical yield.

**What to browse:** Schuylkill County Court of Common Pleas Naturalization Dockets and Declarations on FamilySearch. These volumes are digitized but largely unindexed. Browse the 1845–1860 range for "Flynn."

**What to look for:**
- Thomas Flynn declaration of intent or oath of allegiance
- Country/county/parish of origin in Ireland → opens Irish records research
- Wife's name, children listed

---

#### Priority 4 — Schuylkill County Deed Books (browse around the 1881 deed)

**Why:** The Thomas → Patrick deed (src_008, 1881) is found but the citation is rough. The **Deed Book volume** containing that transaction may show neighboring entries — other Thomas Flynn transactions with other children, or a release of dower rights by Thomas's widow — that corroborate family relationships.

**What to browse:** Browse 5–10 pages before and after the indexed deed entry in the Deed Book volume. Also check the Grantor/Grantee index for other Thomas Flynn entries from the 1860s–1880s.

---

#### Priority 5 — Irish Catholic Parish Registers (once townland is known)

**Why:** Patrick was born in Ireland ~1845. If any of the above records (naturalization, church marriage, will) names Thomas Flynn's parish or townland of origin, the next step is to browse the surviving **Irish Catholic baptism registers** for that parish. The Catholic parish registers for most of Ireland are on microfilm through FamilySearch, many as unindexed images.

**Hold this** until the naturalization or church records give you a parish name — browsing Irish registers without a specific place is not productive.

---

### The Gap: 1870, 1880, 1900 Censuses

These are **indexed**, not unindexed, so they fall to the `search-records` agent rather than browse. But they are flagged as a high-severity gap in the timeline (t_001) and should be searched in parallel with the unindexed browse work. The 1870 and 1880 censuses would show Patrick's own household and possibly still show Thomas Flynn's household, and 1880 introduces the relationship column for the first time.

---

### Summary Table

| # | Record Set | Repository | Browse Target | Why It Matters |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Schuylkill Co. Will Books | FamilySearch | Thomas Flynn will text + estate packet, ~1881 | Names heirs → proves Thomas–Patrick parent-child |
| 2 | St. Mary's Catholic marriage register, Pottsville | FamilySearch | ~1838–1845 entries | Names Patrick's mother |
| 3 | Schuylkill Co. Naturalization Dockets | FamilySearch | Court of Common Pleas, 1845–1860 | Thomas's Irish origin + wife/children |
| 4 | Schuylkill Co. Deed Books | FamilySearch | Volume containing 1881 deed + surrounding entries | Corroborates family relationships |
| 5 | Irish Catholic parish registers | FamilySearch | TBD — wait for townland from records above | Patrick's birth record in Ireland |

quirks: Danish military levy rolls (laegdsruller) begin in 1789 and enroll every male from early childhood under his father's name — each son's entry sits directly beneath the father's, making the rolls DIRECT parentage evidence for a male subject.
Danish naming is patronymic before ~1850: 'Mikkel Nielsen' means Mikkel son of Niels, so the father's given name is Niels — the patronymic alone does not identify which Niels.
Vital events are recorded in parish church books (kirkeboeger); baptism entries name both parents. Civil registration is much later.
The Stagstrup parish register is only ~3% name-indexed on FamilySearch — plan to browse the register images by year rather than rely on the index.

The 'Father of the Bride' Robert Eastham named in that marriage record (a_117) must have been born approximately 1795-1805 to have a daughter old enough to marry in 1844, making him too old to be the Robert Eastham Jr. (b. ~1822, Greenup County) who co-resided with the Burtons in 1850 and 1860.
